questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Reason about why photosynthesis and respiration are complementary processes.
questions.stem: In a ward round, a clinician asks why a plant still needs respiration when it captures light energy; which reasoning is best?

options.text: Respiration releases ATP from sugars that photosynthesis only builds, and runs day and night
Photosynthesis stores energy in sugars, while respiration breaks sugars down to release usable ATP
options.misconception: treats the two processes as serving identical purposes

options.text: Chloroplasts make sugars, while mitochondria provide oxygen for photosynthesis
options.misconception: claims mitochondria supply the oxygen for photosynthesis

options.text: Respiration is needed only in the dark, and photosynthesis replaces it in daylight
options.misconception: believes photosynthesis replaces respiration in daylight

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis stores energy in glucose, but the cell needs ATP in the form respiration can deliver from it. Respiration also runs at night, so both processes are always needed.
questions.hint: One stores energy, the other releases it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the products of the light-dependent reactions.
questions.stem: In a clinic teaching note, the question concerns which substances the light-dependent reactions produce for the Calvin cycle to use.

options.text: Glucose and oxygen, the final products of the whole photosynthetic process
options.misconception: confuses the light stage with the whole process

options.text: ATP and NADPH, which power carbon fixation in the Calvin cycle
Carbon dioxide and water, the raw materials of the photosynthetic reaction
options.misconception: names the reactants as the products

options.text: Pyruvate and carbon dioxide, the products of glycolysis in the cytoplasm
options.misconception: confuses light reactions with glycolysis

questions.explanation: The light-dependent reactions split water, release oxygen and build ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle then uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into carbohydrate.
questions.hint: Which two carriers power the Calvin cycle?

questions.learningObjective: Interpret data on oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide release.
questions.stem: During a ward round, gas exchange data show 18 millilitres of oxygen and 12 of carbon dioxide over an hour; what does the ratio show?

options.text: The sample is photosynthesising fast, since carbon dioxide release is high
options.misconception: reads high carbon dioxide release as photosynthesis

options.text: The sample is fermenting, since oxygen was consumed during the hour
options.misconception: treats any oxygen use as fermentation

options.text: The sample is respiring aerobically, with some oxygen used for non-respiratory work
The sample is dead, because no carbon dioxide was released at all
options.misconception: ignores the carbon dioxide actually released

questions.explanation: Oxygen uptake with carbon dioxide release shows aerobic respiration, and a volume ratio below one is expected when some oxygen feeds other reactions too. Fermentation releases no carbon dioxide.
questions.hint: Oxygen in and carbon dioxide out means aerobic respiration.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why glycolysis can run without oxygen.
questions.stem: A patient asks why glycolysis still proceeds when oxygen tension is very low; explain the reason.

answer.exemplar: Glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate using only enzymes already present in the cytoplasm, so it needs no oxygen directly. It yields a small amount of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, which is enough to keep running when oxygen is scarce, and the pyruvate can then be fermented to regenerate the NAD needed to keep the pathway going.

questions.explanation: Glycolysis uses cytoplasmic enzymes and produces ATP directly from ADP, so no oxygen is required. Oxygen is needed only later for aerobic respiration, and fermentation regenerates the NAD.
questions.hint: Oxygen is not a reactant in this pathway.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate ATP use per turn of the Calvin cycle.
questions.stem: One tracer study recorded 90 micromoles of ATP consumed while the Calvin cycle turned 30 times in a minute.
questions.explanation: Dividing 90 micromoles of ATP by 30 turns gives 3 micromoles per turn, matching the 3 ATP needed for each carbon dioxide fixed. Any other figure misstates the energy cost of fixation.
questions.hint: Divide ATP consumed by number of turns.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage change in a photosynthesis rate.
questions.stem: A plant growth log reports carbon dioxide uptake of 12 micromoles per hour at 20 degrees and 24 at 30; what is the percentage increase in rate?
questions.explanation: The rate rose by 12 micromoles per hour on a starting value of 12, and 12 divided by 12 is 1, so the percentage increase is 100. The rate simply doubled over that ten degree rise.
questions.hint: Percentage rise equals the change over the original value.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about how temperature affects respiration rate.
questions.stem: Consulting notes ask why a warm muscle in a fever respires faster than a cool one; which reasoning is sound?

options.text: Enzymes in respiration work faster as temperature rises, raising the overall rate
Cold muscles need less oxygen, so they must respire more slowly overall
options.misconception: reverses the effect of temperature on respiration

questions.explanation: Respiration is controlled by enzymes, and raising temperature speeds the reactions until they begin to denature. A fever therefore raises metabolic rate, so a hot patient burns more energy.
questions.hint: Enzymes drive respiration, and heat speeds them.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the overall equation of photosynthesis.
questions.stem: A patient's family asks why photosynthesis needs light, carbon dioxide and water; give the overall reasoning.

answer.exemplar: Light energy is needed to split water and charge the carriers ATP and NADPH, and those carriers then power the fixation of carbon dioxide into carbohydrate. With any of the three missing, either the energy supply or the carbon and hydrogen source is unavailable, so no sugar can be built and the process stops.

questions.explanation: The light reactions need photons to split water and make ATP and NADPH, and the Calvin cycle needs those carriers plus carbon dioxide to build carbohydrate. Remove any input and the process breaks.
questions.hint: Trace what each reactant contributes to the process.

questions.explanation: Dividing 8 micromoles of NADPH by 4 micromoles of carbon dioxide gives 2 NADPH per carbon dioxide fixed, which matches the cycle's requirement of two reduced carriers for each fixation step.
questions.hint: Divide NADPH supplied by carbon dioxide fixed.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about what limits the Calvin cycle once light is saturating.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Spot an error in a claim about light and photosynthesis rate.
questions.stem: A clinician's note claims that raising the light level always raises sugar output in a crop; which part of that claim is faulty?

options.text: Only the mention of crops is wrong, since the claim holds for all plants
options.misconception: accepts the claim but narrows it to crops

options.text: Only the mention of sugar is wrong, since light raises glucose alone
options.misconception: accepts the claim but swaps in glucose

options.text: The word always is wrong, since another factor soon becomes limiting instead

questions.explanation: Light is only one limiting factor, so once carbon dioxide, temperature or enzyme supply becomes limiting, more light adds nothing. The claim is not wrong in itself but wrong to say always.
questions.hint: Light stops mattering once something else binds.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how oxygen availability limits the respiration rate.
questions.stem: Another clinician's note asks why a falling blood oxygen level slows a patient's respiration; give the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain, so a lower oxygen level slows the transfer of electrons and reduces the proton gradient that ATP synthase relies on. With less oxidative phosphorylation, the cell leans more on glycolysis and fermentation, which yield far less ATP per glucose and therefore slow the overall rate of respiration.

questions.explanation: Oxygen limits the electron transport chain, so less oxygen means fewer ATP and a slower respiration rate, with more reliance on glycolysis. The cell cannot simply compensate by fermenting faster.
questions.hint: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor in the chain.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate net carbon dioxide uptake accounting for respiration.
questions.stem: One hour of plant gas exchange showed 12 micromoles of carbon dioxide taken in and 8 released by respiration.
questions.explanation: Net uptake is the amount taken in minus the amount released, so 12 minus 8 gives 4 micromoles retained for carbohydrate. Counting only the uptake would overstate the gain by the respiratory loss.
questions.hint: Subtract the released amount from the absorbed amount.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how weak light limits photosynthesis in shaded plants.
questions.stem: A third clinician's note asks why a plant with plenty of water still fails in deep shade; explain the light capture problem.

answer.exemplar: The light-dependent reactions can only use photons in the wavelengths chlorophyll absorbs, so a plant in deep shade both intercepts fewer photons and loses more to leaves that shade one another. With less ATP and NADPH made, the Calvin cycle slows, and the plant cannot compensate for the lost light by taking in more carbon dioxide.

questions.explanation: Shade reduces the photons reaching the leaf and the fraction absorbed, so the light stage makes less ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle is then limited by their supply, not by carbon dioxide.
questions.hint: Fewer usable photons means less ATP and NADPH.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why fermentation sustains glycolysis without oxygen.
questions.stem: A clinician explains why fermenting muscle still makes a little ATP when oxygen is scarce; give the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: Without oxygen the electron transport chain stops, so the only ATP available comes from substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis, which nets two molecules per glucose. Fermentation then converts the pyruvate into lactic acid purely to regenerate the NAD plus that glycolysis needs, so it is a way of keeping the small ATP yield going rather than a source of extra ATP.

questions.explanation: Fermentation itself makes no ATP; it regenerates NAD plus so glycolysis can keep producing two ATP per glucose. Without it the small glycolytic yield would soon stop as well.
questions.hint: Fermentation regenerates NAD, it does not make ATP.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why extra carbon dioxide alone does not lift yield.
questions.stem: A clinician asks whether raising carbon dioxide in a glasshouse always lifts crop yield; give the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: The rate of photosynthesis is set by whichever factor is in shortest supply, and in a glasshouse light is often the limiting one, so extra carbon dioxide simply cannot be fixed. Raising carbon dioxide helps only when light, temperature and enzyme supply are already high enough, which is why growers adjust several factors together rather than one at a time.

questions.explanation: Only the factor that is limiting sets the rate, so extra carbon dioxide is wasted when light or temperature is already limiting. That is why growers change several conditions together.
questions.hint: The limiting factor decides the rate.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain where each stage of aerobic respiration takes place.
questions.stem: A clinician's note asks a student to describe where each stage of aerobic respiration takes place; give the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, where glucose is split into pyruvate with a small gain of ATP. Pyruvate then enters the mitochondrial matrix, where the link reaction and the Krebs cycle strip carbon off as carbon dioxide and load carriers with electrons. Those electrons pass down the electron transport chain on the inner membrane, where oxygen is used and most ATP is made.

questions.explanation: The stages are separated by location: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the Krebs cycle in the matrix, and the electron transport chain on the inner membrane. Each stage feeds the next in sequence.
questions.hint: Match each stage to its compartment.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a fever raises the respiration rate.
questions.stem: One clinician's note asks why a patient's respiration rate rises when their body temperature climbs during a fever; give the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: Respiration is driven by enzymes, and a higher temperature speeds every reaction until they begin to denature, so the rate of respiration climbs and more fuel is consumed. That is why a fever raises metabolic rate, and it explains the raised heart rate, faster breathing and weight loss seen in an unresolved fever.

questions.explanation: Respiratory reactions are enzyme-driven, so a rise in temperature accelerates them and lifts the overall respiration rate. The extra fuel demand is why fevers raise heart rate and breathing rate.
questions.hint: Respiration is limited by enzyme speed.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how glycolysis feeds the Krebs cycle.
questions.stem: A further note asks how the products of glycolysis feed into the Krebs cycle; explain the connection between the stages.

answer.exemplar: Glycolysis ends with pyruvate, which is moved into the mitochondrial matrix and, after carbon dioxide is removed, combined with oxaloacetate to form acetyl groups. These acetyl groups then enter the Krebs cycle, so the two stages are linked by the products of one becoming the fuel for the next.

questions.explanation: Glycolysis produces pyruvate, which is decarboxylated into acetyl groups and fed into the Krebs cycle. The stages are connected in sequence, with the output of one supplying the input of the next.
questions.hint: Pyruvate is the link between the two stages.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how weak autumn light reduces energy capture.
questions.stem: A closing note asks why a plant in weak autumn light captures so little energy; explain the effect on the light-dependent stage.

answer.exemplar: As the days shorten and the sun sits lower, each leaf intercepts fewer photons and sees them at a shallower angle, so the light-dependent reactions make less ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle then fixes carbon more slowly, and the plant partly compensates by producing more chlorophyll and repositioning its leaves to catch what light there is.

questions.explanation: Shorter days and a lower sun angle reduce the light reaching each leaf, so the light stage makes less ATP and NADPH and fixation slows. More chlorophyll and leaf repositioning offset the loss.
questions.hint: Fewer photons means less ATP and NADPH.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how glycolysis contributes when carbohydrate intake is low.
questions.stem: A final note asks why a patient on a very low carbohydrate diet can still make a little ATP from protein; explain the role of glycolysis.

answer.exemplar: Protein can be broken down into amino acids, and their carbon skeletons can be converted into intermediates such as pyruvate that enter the pathway. Glycolysis then converts these three-carbon molecules into lactate, regenerating the NAD plus that keeps the route open, so a small amount of ATP is still produced even when dietary carbohydrate is scarce.

questions.explanation: Amino acids from protein can be converted into pyruvate or related intermediates that feed into glycolysis, yielding a small net ATP. Most energy still comes from fat, so this route adds little.
questions.hint: Protein carbon skeletons can enter the pathway.
